chapterTitle: The High Priestly Prayer — When the Son Prayed For You By Name
themeTitle: "Before the Cross, He Prayed Your Name"

scripture.text: Jesus said these things, and lifting up his eyes to heaven, he said, “Father, the time has come. Glorify your Son, that your Son may also glorify you;
scripture.understanding: The hour Jesus spoke of all through John's Gospel — the cross — has finally arrived, and He calls it glory. He does not ask to escape the hour; He asks that through it the Father and the Son would be mutually glorified.

scripture.text: even as you gave him authority over all flesh, so he will give eternal life to all whom you have given him.
scripture.understanding: The Father handed the Son universal authority for one purpose — to give eternal life. Notice the sovereignty: He gives that life 'to all whom you have given him.'

scripture.text: This is eternal life, that they should know you, the only true God, and him whom you sent, Jesus Christ.
scripture.understanding: Here is Jesus' own definition of eternal life — not endless duration but relational knowledge of 'the only true God' and the One He sent. Eternal life is a Person you know, not merely a place you go.

scripture.text: I glorified you on the earth. I have accomplished the work which you have given me to do.
scripture.understanding: Before a single nail is driven, Jesus speaks of the work as finished — such is His confidence in the Father's will. He glorified God not by avoiding the assignment but by completing it.

scripture.text: Now, Father, glorify me with your own self with the glory which I had with you before the world existed.
scripture.understanding: Jesus asks for the restoration of the glory He shared with the Father 'before the world existed' — a direct claim to pre-existent deity. This is the eternal Word of John 1:1 asking to return to the Father's side.

scripture.text: I revealed your name to the people whom you have given me out of the world. They were yours, and you have given them to me. They have kept your word.
scripture.understanding: Jesus sums up His ministry as revealing the Father's 'name' — His very character and being — to the people the Father drew out of the world. The mark of these people: 'they have kept your word.'

scripture.text: Now they have known that all things whatever you have given me are from you,
scripture.understanding: The disciples have finally recognized the divine source of everything in Jesus. Their eyes have opened to see that Jesus is not self-originated but Father-sent.

scripture.text: for the words which you have given me I have given to them, and they received them, and knew for sure that I came from you, and they have believed that you sent me.
scripture.understanding: Faith travels along words: the Father gave words to the Son, the Son gave them to the disciples, and they received, knew, and believed. Belief here rests on the settled certainty that Jesus came from God.

scripture.text: I pray for them. I don’t pray for the world, but for those whom you have given me, for they are yours.
scripture.understanding: Jesus draws a deliberate circle around His own — He is interceding specifically for those the Father has given Him, not making a blanket prayer for the unbelieving world in this moment. His people belong to the Father before they ever belonged to themselves.

scripture.text: All things that are mine are yours, and yours are mine, and I am glorified in them.
scripture.understanding: The seamless sharing of everything between Father and Son — 'yours are mine' — is a claim only deity can make. And astonishingly, Jesus says He is glorified in His people.

scripture.text: I am no more in the world, but these are in the world, and I am coming to you. Holy Father, keep them through your name which you have given me, that they may be one, even as we are.
scripture.understanding: Jesus is leaving; His disciples are staying in a hostile world. So He commits them to the Father's keeping 'through your name,' and asks that their unity would mirror the very oneness of Father and Son.

scripture.text: While I was with them in the world, I kept them in your name. Those whom you have given me I have kept. None of them is lost, except the son of destruction, that the Scripture might be fulfilled.
scripture.understanding: While present, Jesus personally guarded them and lost none — except Judas, whose fall fulfilled Scripture. Judas is called 'the son of destruction,' a man defined by the ruin he chose.

scripture.text: But now I come to you, and I say these things in the world, that they may have my joy made full in themselves.
scripture.understanding: Jesus prays aloud, in their hearing, on purpose — so that His own joy would be reproduced and completed inside them. His joy, not merely relief, is the inheritance He leaves.

scripture.text: I have given them your word. The world hated them, because they are not of the world, even as I am not of the world.
scripture.understanding: The Father's word marks the disciples as not-of-this-world, and that otherness is exactly why the world hates them. To carry His word is to share His alienation.

scripture.text: I pray not that you would take them from the world, but that you would keep them from the evil one.
scripture.understanding: Jesus does not pray for escape or removal from the world but for protection within it — kept from 'the evil one.' Withdrawal is not the plan; guarded presence is.

scripture.text: They are not of the world even as I am not of the world.
scripture.understanding: Jesus repeats it for emphasis: the believer's citizenship is not earthly. Their identity is anchored in Him, not in the world's order.

scripture.text: Sanctify them in your truth. Your word is truth.
scripture.understanding: 'Sanctify' means to set apart as holy, and the instrument is truth — specifically God's word, which Jesus flatly declares to be truth itself. Not that the word merely contains truth; the word is truth.

scripture.text: As you sent me into the world, even so I have sent them into the world.
scripture.understanding: As the Father commissioned the Son into the world, so the Son commissions the disciples. Sanctification is not for seclusion — it is for sending.

scripture.text: For their sakes I sanctify myself, that they themselves also may be sanctified in truth.
scripture.understanding: Jesus consecrates Himself — setting Himself apart for the altar of the cross — so that His people can be truly sanctified. His self-offering is the ground of their holiness.

scripture.text: Not for these only do I pray, but for those also who will believe in me through their word,
scripture.understanding: The prayer widens to include you — everyone who will ever believe through the apostles' message. In the upper room, Jesus was already praying for people not yet born.

scripture.text: that they may all be one; even as you, Father, are in me, and I in you, that they also may be one in us; that the world may believe that you sent me.
scripture.understanding: The goal of unity is named: a oneness modeled on the mutual indwelling of Father and Son, so real that it becomes evidence to the world that the Father sent the Son. Unity is evangelism.

scripture.text: The glory which you have given me, I have given to them; that they may be one, even as we are one;
scripture.understanding: Jesus gives His people the very glory the Father gave Him, and this shared glory is the cement of their oneness. Believers are united not by agreement but by a common glory.

scripture.text: I in them, and you in me, that they may be perfected into one; that the world may know that you sent me, and loved them, even as you loved me.
scripture.understanding: Perfect unity — 'perfected into one' — becomes the world's proof that the Father sent Jesus and loves His people with the same love He has for His Son. The church's oneness preaches the Father's love.

scripture.text: Father, I desire that they also whom you have given me be with me where I am, that they may see my glory, which you have given me, for you loved me before the foundation of the world.
scripture.understanding: Jesus' final request is that His people be with Him to see His glory — a glory rooted in a love that predates creation. This is heaven's essence: to be where He is and behold Him.

scripture.text: Righteous Father, the world hasn’t known you, but I knew you; and these knew that you sent me.
scripture.understanding: Jesus contrasts the world's ignorance of the Father with His own perfect knowledge, and the disciples' knowledge that the Father sent Him. Knowing is the dividing line between the world and the church.

scripture.text: I made known to them your name, and will make it known; that the love with which you loved me may be in them, and I in them.”
scripture.understanding: The prayer ends with a promise of ongoing revelation — Jesus will keep making the Father known — so that the Father's own love, and Jesus Himself, would live inside the believer. The prayer closes not with duty but with indwelling love.

visualMeditations.title: Lifting Up His Eyes to Heaven
visualMeditations.image: Watch the posture. The other Gospels show Jesus in Gethsemane falling on His face, sweating blood, pleading. But John freezes a different frame first — the Master standing in the upper room, or on the road toward the garden, and lifting His eyes up. Not bowing His head in defeat, but raising His face toward the Father as a Son looking straight into the eyes of the One He trusts. The cross is hours away. Judas is already moving in the dark. And Jesus looks up.
visualMeditations.meaning: This is the last long prayer before the arrest, and it is not a prayer of panic. Ancient prayer was often offered with eyes lifted, open, upward — the posture of a Son who has nothing to hide and everything to entrust. Before He faces the worst that hell can do, Jesus fixes His gaze on the Father's face. That is where the strength for your own dark hour comes from — not from staring at the trouble, but from lifting your eyes.

visualMeditations.title: The Glory Before the World Existed
visualMeditations.image: Rewind past Bethlehem. Rewind past the prophets, past Sinai, past the flood, past Eden — past the first word 'Let there be light.' Go back to before there was a 'before,' before a single galaxy hung in the void, and there is the Son, blazing in shared glory with the Father. Now watch that same Person, wearing dusty human feet, ask to have that glory given back. The One who wrapped Himself in flesh is asking to be unwrapped and welcomed home.
visualMeditations.meaning: This is one of the boldest claims of deity in all Scripture. Jesus does not ask for a glory He never had; He asks for the glory He 'had with you before the world existed.' The Word who was with God and was God (John 1:1) is speaking. He laid that visible glory down to save you, and here — on the doorstep of the cross — He asks the Father to restore it. Your salvation cost Him the temporary surrender of heaven's brightness.

visualMeditations.title: Kept Through the Name — None Lost
visualMeditations.image: Picture a shepherd counting his flock through the gate at dusk, one hand on each head as they pass. He is leaving the field; night is coming; wolves are near. So he presses each animal into the care of a stronger keeper and says, 'Guard them by your name — not one of them is missing.' The Greek word for 'keep' is a watchman's word: eyes fixed, guarding from loss, holding fast. Jesus has been that watchman for three years, and He has lost none — except the one who walked out into the night on his own feet.
visualMeditations.meaning: This is the security of the believer painted in a single image. Jesus kept His own in the Father's name and lost none of them. Judas is the tragic exception — 'the son of destruction' — but he was never truly given; he was a thief and a betrayer who chose his ruin. For everyone the Father has genuinely given the Son, the message is unshakeable: you are guarded by the name of God Himself, and no wolf can snatch you out of that hand.

visualMeditations.title: That They May All Be One
visualMeditations.image: Imagine three rings interlocking so tightly you cannot tell where one ends and the next begins — the Father in the Son, the Son in the Father, and then, impossibly, you drawn inside the circle: 'they also may be one in us.' Jesus is not praying for a committee that agrees on paperwork. He is praying that believers would be woven into the same living oneness that has bound Father and Son from eternity, and that the watching world would see the seam-less unity and conclude: only God could make people love like that.
visualMeditations.meaning: The unity Jesus prays for is not organizational sameness; it is a shared life flowing from the Trinity into the church. And it has a missionary purpose stated twice — 'that the world may believe' and 'that the world may know.' The oneness of Christians is the final apologetic. When the world sees people who should be divided — by race, class, history, temperament — bound in real love, it becomes proof that the Father sent the Son. Your unity with other believers is not optional niceness; it is evangelism the world cannot argue with.

structure.label: Jesus Prays for Himself (v. 1-5)
structure.body: 'Glorify your Son' — the hour of the cross is the hour of glory, and eternal life is defined as knowing the only true God.

structure.label: Jesus Prays for His Disciples (v. 6-19)
structure.body: Keep them, guard them from the evil one, and sanctify them in the truth of your word — then send them into the world as you sent me.

structure.label: Jesus Prays for All Who Will Believe (v. 20-26)
structure.body: That they may all be one as the Father and Son are one, perfected in unity so the world believes, and finally be with Him to see His glory.

sections.heading: The High Priest at His Own Altar
paragraphs: For sixteen chapters John has been building to an hour. 'My hour has not yet come,' Jesus kept saying (2:4; 7:30; 8:20). Now, in the shadow of Gethsemane, He lifts His eyes and says the opposite: 'Father, the time has come.' And John frames what follows not as a teaching but as a prayer — the longest recorded prayer of Jesus in the Gospels. It has been called, rightly, the High Priestly Prayer, because here Jesus does exactly what Israel's high priest did on the Day of Atonement: he stands between God and the people, carrying their names into the presence of the Father, on the eve of a sacrifice. The difference is staggering — this High Priest is also the Lamb.

The whole prayer moves outward in three widening circles. First Jesus prays for Himself (v. 1-5) — not for rescue, but for glory, and He redefines glory as the cross. Then He prays for the eleven men in the room (v. 6-19) — that they be kept, guarded, and sanctified. Then, in the most tender turn in the chapter, He prays 'for those also who will believe in me through their word' (v. 20) — which means He prayed for you, by anticipation, in that room, before you drew a single breath. The prayer that carried the disciples through the fire was already reaching two thousand years down to carry you.

sections.heading: Eternal Life Is a Person, Not a Length
paragraphs: Verse 3 is one of the most important definitions in the Bible, and Jesus gives it in His own words: 'This is eternal life, that they should know you, the only true God, and him whom you sent, Jesus Christ.' Notice what He does not say. He does not say eternal life is a duration (living forever), or a location (going to heaven), or a reward (streets of gold). He says eternal life is knowing — a present, relational, experiential knowing of God. The Greek word is not the knowing of a fact but the knowing of a face. This means eternal life is not only something you receive when you die; it is something you begin the moment you truly know God through Jesus Christ. If you know Him, eternity has already started in you.

This is also the quiet demolition of every religion that offers God without Jesus. Jesus binds them together — to know 'the only true God' is inseparable from knowing 'him whom you sent, Jesus Christ.' You cannot have the Father while bypassing the Son. And in the same breath Jesus calls Himself 'Jesus Christ' and speaks of the glory He shared with the Father 'before the world existed' (v. 5) — an unmistakable claim to be the eternal God in flesh. The prayer that defines eternal life also settles who Jesus is: not a way to God among many, but the only Son sent from the Father's side.

sections.heading: Sanctified in Truth, Sent Into the World
paragraphs: The prayer for the disciples turns on two verbs. First, 'keep them' (v. 11, 15) — a watchman's word for guarding from loss and from the evil one. Jesus does not pray that they be taken out of the world (v. 15); escapism is not the plan. He prays that they be guarded within it. Then, 'Sanctify them in your truth. Your word is truth' (v. 17). To sanctify is to set apart as holy, and the instrument God uses is His word — which Jesus does not say contains truth but flatly is truth. The believer is made holy not by retreating from reality but by being saturated in the Word until it separates them, from the inside, unto God.

And sanctification is never for hiding. 'As you sent me into the world, even so I have sent them into the world' (v. 18). You are not set apart to sit in a holy huddle; you are set apart to be launched. The pattern is exact: the sanctified Son was sent, so the sanctified church is sent. And it is grounded in verse 19 — 'For their sakes I sanctify myself' — where Jesus consecrates Himself to the altar so that His people can be truly made holy. His self-offering is the reason your sanctification is even possible.

ntConnection.heading: New Testament Connection
paragraphs: John 17 is not a one-time event that ended when Jesus said 'Amen.' It is the earthly opening of a ministry Jesus has never stopped performing. The book of Hebrews lifts the curtain on what happened after the cross and resurrection: 'Therefore he is also able to save to the uttermost those who draw near to God through him, seeing that he lives forever to make intercession for them' (Hebrews 7:25). The High Priest who lifted His eyes and prayed for His people in the upper room now stands in the true holy place and prays for them still. Romans 8:34 nails it shut: 'It is Christ who died, yes rather, who was raised from the dead, who is at the right hand of God, who also makes intercession for us.'

Put those together and the pastoral force is overwhelming. When Jesus prayed in verse 20 for 'those also who will believe in me through their word,' He was not saying a nice thing that expired that night — He was beginning a prayer He is still praying over your name today. The reason you have not fallen away, the reason the evil one has not snatched you, the reason you are still kept, is not the strength of your grip on Him but the intercession of the One at the Father's right hand who never stops praying you home. John 17 is a window into what your Savior is doing for you this very hour.

lexicon.insight: From dóxa (G1391), glory. The word means to render or esteem as glorious, to clothe in visible splendor. The shock of John 17 is what Jesus counts as glory: not escape from the cross but the cross itself. 'Father, the time has come. Glorify your Son' — and the hour He is asking to be glorified in is the hour of His crucifixion. In John's Gospel, the cross is the throne. And then Jesus dares to say He has given that same glory to His people (v. 22). The path to glory, for the Master and for you, runs straight through surrender.

To know — not the cold storage of information but the warm knowledge of relationship and experience, the same word used for the deepest intimacy between persons. This is the word Jesus chooses to define eternal life in verse 3: 'that they should know you.' Eternal life is not knowing about God; it is knowing God. Verse 25 draws the dividing line of the universe with this word — 'the world hasn't known you, but I knew you' — and the church stands on the knowing side. Do you know Him, or do you only know things about Him?

A watchman's word — to guard from loss or injury by keeping your eye on something, to hold fast, to watch over. It is what a sentry does through the long night. Jesus uses it of His own past care ('I kept them,' v. 12) and of His request for the future ('keep them,' v. 11, 15). The security of the believer lives inside this verb: you are not merely saved, you are guarded — watched over by the Father's own name against the evil one. And notice the reciprocity: the disciples 'have kept your word' (v. 6). The ones God guards are the ones who guard His word.

From hágios, holy — to make holy, to set apart, to consecrate. It is a temple word: a vessel is sanctified when it is separated from common use and dedicated wholly to God. Jesus prays 'Sanctify them in your truth' and names the instrument in the same breath: 'Your word is truth' — alḗtheia (G225), reality as opposed to falsehood and pretense. God does not make you holy by feelings or by hiding; He does it by His word, which is truth itself, separating you from the inside out. And Jesus sanctifies Himself first (v. 19) — sets Himself apart to the cross — so that your holiness has a foundation to stand on.

The simple numeral 'one' — but Jesus loads it with the weight of the Trinity. He does not pray that believers merely cooperate or agree; He prays that they be one 'even as we are' (v. 11), one 'even as you, Father, are in me, and I in you' (v. 21). The measure of Christian unity is the oneness of the Father and the Son. And its purpose is missionary, stated twice: 'that the world may believe' (v. 21) and 'that the world may know' (v. 23). Your oneness with other believers is not sentimental — it is the argument that convinces the world Jesus is real.

holySpiritRevelation.intro: The Spirit is dealing with three things you may have never let land: that Jesus prayed for you personally, that eternal life is available to you right now, and that you are being kept by a power stronger than your own grip.

items.title: You Were on His Mind Before the Nail
items.body: Read verse 20 slowly: 'Not for these only do I pray, but for those also who will believe in me through their word.' That is you. On the most agonizing night of His life, hours from betrayal, scourging, and crucifixion, Jesus lifted His eyes and prayed for people who did not yet exist — and He meant you. You were not an afterthought of the gospel; you were a named request in the Savior's prayer before you were born. So let it hit you: when have you ever prayed for someone you had never met, on the worst night of your life? He did. Do you live like someone who was prayed for by name?

items.title: Eternal Life You Can Have Right Now
items.body: You have been taught to think of eternal life as something that starts when you die. Jesus corrects you in verse 3: 'This is eternal life, that they should know you.' Eternal life is a relationship, and relationships happen in the present tense. That means the abundance of eternity is not only ahead of you in a distant heaven — it is available the moment you truly know God through Jesus Christ. Are you settling for knowing about Him — facts, doctrines, church attendance — when He is offering you the thing itself: to know Him? What would change this week if you treated eternal life as a Person to be known today rather than a destination to be reached someday?

items.title: You Are Kept
items.body: 'Holy Father, keep them... I kept them... None of them is lost' (v. 11-12). The word is a watchman's word — He guards you like a sentry through the night. You are not held in the faith by the strength of your own willpower; you are held by the name of God. The evil one is real (v. 15), the world's hatred is real (v. 14), but so is this: you are guarded. Judas was lost because he was a thief who chose the dark, not because the Shepherd's grip failed. So when you feel like you are barely hanging on, remember Who is actually doing the holding. Will you rest today in the fact that your security is His job, not yours?

audit.title: The Knowing vs. Knowing-About Check
audit.body: Jesus said eternal life is to know God (v. 3). Be brutally honest: do you actually know Him, or do you only know a great deal about Him? Could you describe a real conversation with God this week, or only recite facts, verses, and opinions? Information about a person is not intimacy with them.

audit.title: The 'One' Test
audit.body: Jesus prayed four times that His people would be one (v. 11, 21, 22, 23), and He made it the proof to the world that He is real. So look at your own life in the body of Christ: are you a source of unity or a source of division? Is there a believer you are quietly at war with, gossiping about, or refusing to forgive — and does your disunity make the gospel harder to believe for someone watching?

audit.title: The 'In, Not Of' Audit
audit.body: Jesus refused to pray that you be taken out of the world (v. 15); He prayed that you be sanctified and sent into it (v. 17-18). So which drift have you fallen into — hiding from the world in a holy huddle, or blending into it until you look no different? Are you 'in the world' but not 'of it,' or have you collapsed one side of that into the other?

practices.title: Pray John 17 Back Over Yourself
practices.body: This week, take your Bible and read John 17 out loud as a prayer — but when you reach verse 20, stop and insert your own name: 'You prayed for me, that I would believe through their word.' Then pray verses 11-17 back to the Father for yourself and for your church by name: 'Keep me. Guard me from the evil one. Sanctify me in Your truth.' Let the Savior's prayer become your prayer.

practices.title: Repair One Break in the Body
practices.body: Because unity is the world's proof that Jesus is real (v. 21, 23), pick one fractured relationship with another believer and take a concrete step toward oneness this week. Send the message, make the call, ask forgiveness, or extend it. Do not wait to feel like it — obey the prayer of Jesus and act. Then watch what it does to your own heart.

prayerReflection: "Father, the time has come for me to hear this prayer as my own. I thank You that before I ever drew a breath, Jesus lifted His eyes to heaven and prayed for me — for the one who would believe through the apostles' word. Let that settle into my bones: I was named in the Savior's prayer. Lord Jesus, You said eternal life is to know the only true God and You whom He sent — so I refuse to settle for knowing about You. I want to know You. Draw me past information into intimacy. Holy Father, keep me through Your name; guard me from the evil one; do not let me be lost. Sanctify me in Your truth, for Your word is truth — set me apart and send me into the world, not out of it. Make me one with Your people, even as You and the Son are one, that the watching world would believe You are real. And Lord, let the love with which the Father loved the Son be in me, and Christ Himself in me, until I am with You where You are and see Your glory. In Jesus' name, Amen."

storyConnections.title: The High Priest's Breastplate — Names Carried Into the Presence
storyConnections.summary: God commanded that Israel's high priest wear a breastplate set with twelve engraved stones, one for each tribe, 'over his heart, when he goes in to the holy place, for a memorial before the LORD continually' (Exodus 28:29). On the Day of Atonement he entered the Most Holy Place carrying the names of the people on his very heart, before God. In John 17 Jesus does precisely this — He carries His people into the Father's presence, praying for those the Father has given Him, keeping them in the divine name. But this High Priest does not merely wear the names; He is about to shed His own blood for them, making Himself both the priest who intercedes and the Lamb who is offered.

storyConnections.title: Moses Interceding on the Mountain
storyConnections.summary: After Israel worshiped the golden calf, Moses climbed back up the mountain and threw himself between God's wrath and the people: 'Yet now, if you will, forgive their sin — and if not, please blot me out of your book which you have written.' The mediator offered himself for the people he prayed for. Jesus stands in that same gap in John 17, praying for His own and then going further than Moses ever could — not merely offering to be blotted out, but actually being blotted out under the judgment His people deserved. Where Moses pleaded for mercy, Jesus purchased it, sanctifying Himself for their sakes (v. 19) so that they could be made holy.
